title: Como decía mi abuela
desc: Quoting the dead to end an argument
setting: Two months of argument about the old house, and doña Elena has just started telling a story instead.

steps.speaker: Doña Elena
steps.es: Mi mamá crió cinco hijos en esa casa.
steps.en: My mother raised five children in that house.

options.feedback: She has stopped arguing and started telling. The story is the argument now, and interrupting it loses it.
True, and it hurries a woman who has waited two months to say it.

options.es: Pero eso no cambia los números.
options.en: But that does not change the numbers.
options.feedback: It is about to change everything. You have just told the room you cannot hear it coming.

steps.speaker: Doña Elena
steps.es: Como decía mi mamá, una casa no se vende.
steps.en: As my mother used to say, a house is not sold.

options.feedback: Nobody argues with a dead grandmother. Silence here is agreement and everybody in the room understands it.
Agreement out loud. Slightly more than the moment needs, but harmless.

options.en: And did she really say that?
options.feedback: Asking whether the quote is real is the one question that cannot be asked.
The argument is over and Julio said so by asking about the rice. Taking the plate is how you agree.
Fine. Somebody has to make the new subject work and it is easier with two.
It was decided. Asking makes her say it a second time.

steps.speaker: Lucía
steps.es: (en el carro) ¿Vos creés que la abuela dijo eso?
steps.en: (in the car) Do you think her grandmother said that?

options.es: Puede que sí o puede que no. Igual era lo que pensaba.
options.en: She may have or she may not. It was what she thought either way.
options.feedback: You understood that the quote finishes an idea the dead woman never put into a sentence. That is exactly how it works here.
Honest. It sidesteps a question she was actually asking you.
Perhaps. Saying it out loud makes what happened smaller than it was.
